title: Declining Offers Without Damaging Relationships
titleEs: Rechazar ofrecimientos sin dañar la relación
summary: Say no to a generous offer and keep the relationship: thanks first, the no early and softened (*I'm afraid we'll have to pass at this stage*), a short reason about the situation (*it would take…, it wouldn't save…*), a smaller yes if you can, and an open door (*if things change, you'll be the first to know*).
canDo: Decline an offer or an invitation in five moves: thanks, the no, the reason, an alternative and an open door.
Present the no as forced by the situation (*we'll have to pass*, *not in a position to*, *at this stage*), not as a judgement on the offer.
Explain the cost of saying yes with *would* (the imagined acceptance) and promise with *will* (the open door).
Say *thanks for*, *but I'm afraid* and *I'd love to* with their weak forms, and keep *to* strong at the end.

focus.grammar: Ellipsis with to (I'd love to, but…) · would for an imagined acceptance (it would take, it wouldn't save) · first conditional for the open door (if things change, you'll…) · thanks for + -ing · not in a position to + verb
focus.lexis: thanks for thinking of us, that's really kind of you, I'd love to but, I'm afraid we'll have to pass, not in a position to, at this stage, bring someone up to speed, leave the door open, take a rain check, we've got it covered, decline
focus.afh: weak forms: for /fə(r)/, but /bət/ · to weak /tə/ before a verb but strong /tuː/ at the end (I'd love to) · thanks /θ/ · deCLINE · appreciate /əˈpriː.ʃi.eɪt/ with /ʃ/

warmup: Remember an invitation or an offer you turned down. How did you say no? Did the other person offer again later? What, in your words, kept the door open or closed it?

organizer.title: The five moves of a safe no
organizer.prompt: Name the move in each part of Ryan's email.

organizer.explain: Thanks → the no, early and softened → a reason about the situation → a smaller yes → the open door. The no comes in the second sentence, not at the end.

questions.q: Ryan writes *we'll have to pass on it at this stage*. What does *at this stage* add? And how is *we'll have to pass* different from *we don't want it* or *we don't need it*?
questions.model: *At this stage* limits the no to the present moment of the project: the problem is the timing, not the offer, so the answer could change later. *We'll have to pass* presents the no as something the situation forces on the team (*have to*), not as a preference. *We don't want it* or *we don't need it* would sound like a judgement on the offer, and indirectly on Helen, who made it.
criteria: You said *at this stage* limits the no to now and suggests it could change.
You said *have to* makes the no sound forced by the situation, not chosen.
You said *we don't want / need it* would judge the offer and the person who made it.

questions.q: Compare *Their access would take about two weeks*, *it wouldn't save us any time* and *If things change, you'll be the first to know*. Why does Ryan use *would* in the first two and *will* in the third? Write the patterns.

signals.re: imagin|hypothet|unreal|if we accepted|if we said yes|not going to
signals.label: would = imagined yes

questions.model: The first two describe an imagined situation, the one in which Ryan says yes, which is not going to happen: *would / wouldn't* + bare infinitive, with an unspoken *if we accepted*. That is a hidden Second Conditional, and it makes the reason sound hypothetical and soft. The third is a real possibility in the future: *if* + present simple, *will* + bare infinitive (First Conditional). *Will* makes the promise firm.
criteria: You said *would* describes the imagined acceptance (an unspoken *if we accepted*).
You said *will* describes a real future possibility, a firm promise.
You wrote the patterns: *would* + bare infinitive; *if* + present simple, *will* + bare infinitive.

questions.q: Helen offered two developers at no cost. Why does Ryan ask for something smaller (*a quick line to your data team*) after saying no? How might Helen feel if the email ended after the reason?

signals.label: ending at the reason feels cold

questions.model: A plain no to a generous offer can feel like a rejection of the person. By declining the big offer and asking for something smaller that really helps, Ryan accepts Helen's goodwill, keeps her involved and shows that the no is about timing, not about her. If the email ended after the reason, it would be logical but cold: Helen might feel her help was not wanted, and next time she might not offer. The open door (*you'll be the first to know*) protects the relationship for later.
criteria: You said the smaller request accepts Helen's goodwill and keeps her involved.
You said an email ending at the reason would feel cold, as if her help were unwanted.
You linked the open door to the future of the relationship.

points: A relationship-safe no has five moves: thanks → the no, early and softened → a short reason about the situation → if possible, a smaller yes → an open door.
Make the no sound forced by the circumstances: *we'll have to pass*, *we're not in a position to*, *at this stage*. Avoid judging the offer (*we don't need it*, *it isn't useful*).
The reason often uses *would* for the imagined yes (*it would take two weeks*, *it wouldn't save us any time*). The open door uses *will*: *if things change, you'll be the first to know*.
Say no clearly, once. Repeating *sorry* or explaining too much sounds unsure and invites the other person to insist.
formulas: Thanks for + noun / -ing; I'm afraid we'll have to pass (on it) at this stage
it would + verb / it wouldn't + verb (= if we accepted)
What would really help is + noun · If + present simple, … will + verb
rule.note: Spanish often builds up slowly before the *no*. In English, the no comes early, usually in the second sentence, and the reason is short: one or two facts. A long justification sounds defensive.

discovery.tts: Hi Helen, thank you so much [for](/fəɹ/) the offer [of](/əv/) Mark [and](/ənd/) Julia; it's really generous. I'm afraid we'll have to pass on it [at](/ət/) this stage, though. Their access [would](/wəd/) take about two weeks to set up, [and](/ənd/) we'd need the third week to bring them up to speed, so it wouldn't save us any time. What [would](/wəd/) really help is a quick line to your data team: answers within a day. [Could](/kəd/) we arrange that? If things change, you'll be the first to know. Best, Ryan

phonetics.intro: Para decir que no con amabilidad usarás tres bloques muy frecuentes: *thanks for…*, *I'd love to…* y *…but I'm afraid…*. En los tres, la palabra funcional se reduce: *for* /fə(r)/, *to* /tə/, *but* /bət/. Hay una excepción importante: cuando *to* queda al final, sin verbo detrás (*I'd love to*), recupera la vocal plena, /tuː/.

items.meaning: a warm opening before a polite no

alerts.text: *For* es /fər/ (US) o /fə/ (UK): «fər», con schwa. *Of* es /əv/ y *us*, /əs/. No «for», «of», «us» con vocales plenas.
/θ/ en *thanks* y *thinking*: la lengua entre los dientes, como la z de España. No «tanks» ni «sanks».
*Thinking of us* va en un bloque: «ZÍN-ki-ŋə-vəs». La ng es /ŋ/, como la n de *tengo*: no añadas una g fuerte delante de *of*.

Sin verbo detrás (al final o antes de una pausa), *to* es fuerte, /tuː/: «aid-LAV-tuu». Escucha las dos variantes.
*Love* lleva /ʌ/, una a breve y central: «LAV». No «lov» con o.

alerts.text: *But* es /bət/: «bət», con schwa. No «BAT» ni «but» con u española.
En EE. UU., la t de *but* entre vocales suena como una r simple: «bə-RAIM». En Reino Unido, t suave: «bə-TAIM».
*Afraid* empieza con schwa y lleva el acento en la segunda sílaba: «ə-FREID», con fr como en *fresa*.

alerts.text: Acento en la segunda sílaba: di-KLAIN. El español «declinar» lo lleva al final.
La primera vocal es /ɪ/, breve y relajada: «di», no «de». La segunda es el diptongo /aɪ/: «KLAIN».
*Declined* es /dɪˈklaɪnd/: tras n, -ed suena /d/ y no añade sílaba: «di-KLAIND», no «di-KLAI-ned».

l1.title: I'd love, but…
l1.text: Spanish *me encantaría, pero…* needs no particle. In English, *to* must stay: it stands for the verb.
l1.wrong: I'd love, but I'm away that weekend.
l1.right: I'd love to, but I'm away that weekend.

l1.title: Assist for «asistir»
l1.text: *Assist* means to help. To go to a meeting or an event is *attend*.
l1.wrong: I'm afraid I can't assist the meeting on Friday.
l1.right: I'm afraid I can't attend the meeting on Friday.

l1.title: Thanks for + base form
l1.text: After a preposition (*for*), the verb takes *-ing*.
l1.wrong: Thanks for invite me, but I can't come.
l1.right: Thanks for inviting me, but I can't come.

l1.title: Reject for «rechazar»
l1.text: *Reject* is harsh: it suits a proposal you judge as bad, not a kind offer. For a polite no, use *decline* or *turn down*.
l1.right: We'll have to decline your kind offer.

l1.title: Too many sorries
l1.text: One *sorry* or *I'm afraid* is enough. Repeating it makes the no sound unsure and invites the other person to insist.
l1.wrong: Sorry, really sorry, we can't, sorry about that.
l1.right: I'm afraid we can't, but thank you for asking.

task.title: Declining a supplier's goodwill offer
task.scenario: Help-center project, a week before launch. After the template problem, Tom's agency offers to add a free chatbot to the help center before the launch, as a goodwill gesture. Any chatbot needs a legal review, which takes about three weeks, and nobody would have time to test it. What you really need from Tom is the template fix by Wednesday. Write the email that says no and keeps Tom on your side.
task.brief: Decline a generous offer in five moves, with *would* for the cost of saying yes and *will* for the open door.
steps: Thank Tom and show you appreciate the offer.
Say no clearly once, softened (*at this stage*).
Give one or two reasons about the situation, with *would*.
Ask for something smaller that would really help.

parts.text: Hi Tom, {{thanks for}} the offer of a free chatbot for the help center; it's {{really generous}}, especially after this week. {{I'm afraid}} {{we'll have to pass}} on it {{at this stage}}, though. Any chatbot needs a legal review, which {{would take}} about three weeks, and we {{wouldn't}} have time to test it properly before the launch. {{What would really help is}} the template fix by Wednesday. {{If things change}} after the launch, {{you'll be the first to know}}: a chatbot could be a good fit for phase two. Best, Alex
parts.label: Declining a goodwill offer (neutral email)
notes: *Thanks for the offer…; it's really generous, especially after this week*: the appreciation is specific, so it sounds sincere.
*I'm afraid we'll have to pass on it at this stage*: the no comes in the second sentence, softened and limited to now.
*Would take about three weeks* and *wouldn't have time*: the imagined yes, with *would*. The reason is about the situation (legal review, testing), not the chatbot.
*What would really help is the template fix by Wednesday*: a smaller, useful yes, with a date.
*If things change… you'll be the first to know* and *phase two*: the open door, with *will*.

parts.speaker: emma
parts.text: {{Thank you for your generous offer}}; {{unfortunately}}, {{we are not in a position to}} accept it before the launch, but {{we would welcome a proposal}} for the second phase.
parts.label: The formal version (letter style)
notes: *Thank you for your generous offer*: full forms and a formal adjective.
*We are not in a position to accept it*: the formal no; the circumstances decide.
*We would welcome a proposal for the second phase*: the open door as a formal invitation.

selfCheck.text: Imagina que eres Tom. Después de leer el correo, ¿volverías a ofrecer ayuda en el futuro? ¿Qué frase concreta te deja con ganas de hacerlo?
¿El tono es cordial y profesional (*thanks for*, *I'm afraid*) sin pasar al chat (*I'll pass*, *rain check*)? ¿Dijiste que no una sola vez y con claridad?
¿Usaste *would* para el sí imaginado (*it would take*, *we wouldn't have time*) y *if* + presente + *will* para la puerta abierta? ¿*Thanks for* va seguido de sustantivo o de *-ing*?
¿Escribiste *I'd love, but*, *assist* por «asistir», *thanks for invite* o *reject* para una oferta amable? Debe ser *I'd love to, but*, *attend*, *thanks for inviting* y *decline / turn down*.
¿Cuántas razones diste? Si fueron más de dos, ¿cuál podrías quitar sin perder nada? Una negativa con demasiadas explicaciones suena a excusa.
